# How to Spot a Phishing Email or Scam Text Before You Click

> **In short:** Don't click and don't reply. Check the message for the warning signs, then contact the company or person using a phone number or website you already know is real — not the details in the message. Report it, then delete it. An AI assistant can help explain a message, but it can't tell you who really sent it.

That "wait, something feels off" feeling when a strange email or text arrives is worth listening to. Phishing messages are fake emails and texts that try to trick you into handing over passwords, account numbers or money, often by pretending to be a company you know. This guide gives you a calm routine for any suspicious message: read it, check the warning signs, verify it another way, and report it. Step 4 is an optional extra on using an AI assistant as a second pair of eyes — handy for explanations, but never a replacement for checking with the real company.

## Before you start
- The suspicious message, open on your screen, with no links tapped, no attachments opened and no replies sent.
- A way to reach the company or person through a phone number or website you already know is real (for example, one printed on a bill or on the back of your card).
- Roughly 5 minutes.
- Optional: an AI assistant you already use, for Step 4.

## Step 1 — Stop and read the message calmly
Open the suspicious email or text and do exactly one thing: read it from top to bottom without tapping anything. Notice three things — a sender or number you don't recognize, a tone that pushes you to act right now, and any link or attachment you weren't expecting. The message looks exactly as it normally would; nothing has changed yet.
💬 Example: "Your package is delayed, confirm here: example.com/track". Just read the words. Don't tap the link.
You'll know it worked when you can describe the message in one short sentence without having clicked anything.

## Step 2 — Check it against the warning signs
The FTC describes four signs of a scam: the sender pretends to be from an organization you know, says there's a problem or a prize, pressures you to act immediately, and insists you pay in a specific way — such as cryptocurrency, a wire transfer, a payment app or gift cards. For phishing messages in particular, the FTC says to watch for claims of suspicious activity, a problem with your account or an invoice you don't recognize, and for requests to confirm personal information or click a payment link. Its example shows a generic greeting and a claimed billing hold, and it points out that legitimate companies won't email or text you a link to update your payment information. CISA lists similar signs: urgent or emotional language, requests for personal or financial information, untrusted shortened links, and incorrect email addresses or links, such as a misspelled company name. CISA also notes that bad grammar is no longer a reliable sign, because AI tools can write text with perfect grammar and spelling.
💬 Example: "Dear customer, your account is on hold because of a billing problem. Update your payment information within 24 hours: example.com/billing". It has a generic greeting, a problem, a deadline and a link to update payment details — several warning signs in two sentences.
You'll know it worked when you can name at least two warning signs in the message, or can say it shows none and you still plan to verify it in Step 3.

## Step 3 — Ask whether you know the sender, then verify another way
The FTC suggests asking yourself whether you have an account with this company, or know the person who contacted you. If not, it may be phishing: report the message and delete it. If you do, contact the company using a phone number or website you know is real, not the information in the message. CISA adds: don't reply, and don't click any attachment or link — including an "unsubscribe" link. Links and attachments can install harmful software. And whoever the message claims to be from, anyone who insists you pay with gift cards, cryptocurrency, a wire transfer or a payment app is a scammer.
You'll know it worked when you have either decided the message is not from anyone you know, or checked it with the real company or person through a channel you already trust.

## Step 4 — Optional: ask an AI assistant to explain the message
If you'd like a second pair of eyes, an AI assistant can walk you through a message's warning signs in plain language. Treat this as an optional extra: the official advice above doesn't depend on it, an assistant only sees the text you paste in and can't confirm who really sent the message, and it can be wrong in either direction. A "this looks fine" answer is never permission to click — Step 3 still applies. Before you paste, remove your own name, address, account numbers, passwords and verification codes, because anything you send into a chat is processed by that service.
💬 Example prompt: "Here is a message I received. Without clicking anything, explain which warning signs of phishing or a scam it shows, if any, and remind me how to check it safely."
You'll know it worked when the answer points to specific parts of the message that you can see yourself — and you still verify it with the real company or person.

## Step 5 — Report it, then delete it
Reporting helps protect other people too. The FTC suggests: forward a phishing email to the Anti-Phishing Working Group at reportphishing@apwg.org; forward a phishing text to 7726 (SPAM); use the report option in your email or messaging app (look for report junk or report spam); and report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov. You can also file a report with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. Outside the US, contact your local police or consumer protection agency. Once you've reported it, delete the message.
You'll know it worked when the message is reported and gone from your inbox, and you haven't tapped anything in it.

## Step 6 — If you already clicked, replied or paid
Don't panic — there are clear next steps. If you clicked a link or opened an attachment, the FTC says to update your security software, run a scan and remove anything it flags as a problem. If you gave out information such as a Social Security, credit card or bank account number, go to IdentityTheft.gov for steps based on what you shared. If you gave out a password, create a new strong one, change it anywhere else you used it, and turn on two-factor authentication. If you paid, act fast: contact the company you paid with — your bank, card company, payment app or the gift card's issuer, using the number on the back of the card — tell them it was a scam and ask about getting the money back. Then report the message as in Step 5.
You'll know it worked when you've taken the steps that match what happened and reported it.

## Common mistakes
- Using the phone number or link in the suspicious message to "check" it — those details come from the sender. Look up the company's contact details yourself, on a website or bill you already trust.
- Replying, or tapping "unsubscribe", to make it stop — CISA's advice is to delete the message without replying or clicking anything in it.
- Treating the AI's answer as the final word — it can miss things or flag the wrong ones. If the message feels off but the assistant says it's fine, trust your gut and verify with the real company.
- Pasting personal details along with the message — your name, address, passwords, codes and account numbers aren't needed to talk through the warning signs; remove them first.
- Relying on typos alone — a message with perfect spelling and grammar can still be a scam.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Slowing down before you click is the most useful habit, because scammers rely on pressure to act immediately. The FTC also recommends multi-factor authentication, which makes it harder for scammers to log in to your accounts even if they have your username and password.
- **For your work:** If a suspicious email arrives at work, follow your employer's process for reporting phishing — usually that means telling your IT or security team — instead of clicking or replying.
- **If you're just getting started:** Try the routine on the very next odd message you receive. You don't need to be perfect; you only need to pause before you click.

## Try it now
The next time an email or text feels off, don't tap anything: run Steps 2 and 3, then report it as in Step 5. While you're at it, switch on multi-factor authentication for one important account today.
